title: Meridian News Authority Broadcast Infrastructure: The Architecture of Sanctioned Information
body:
The Meridian News Authority (MNA) operates as the dominant licensed broadcast entity across the megacity's eleven administrative sectors, holding a Class-I Editorial Charter granted jointly by the Corporate Sovereignty Compact in 2171. Its physical infrastructure — a cluster of transmission towers anchored to the former CN Tower remnant in the Toronto-Hamilton Corridor — distributes content across seventeen simultaneous feed layers, each calibrated to a specific citizenship tier. Tier-1 subscribers receive uncompressed high-fidelity neural-compatible streams with full contextual metadata overlays, while Tier-4 residents receive compressed audio-visual packets stripped of interactive annotation. The difference is not merely cosmetic: lower tiers receive fewer sourced citations, fewer corrections, and a narrower range of permitted commentary topics. This stratification is not hidden — it is contractual.

The MNA does not describe itself as a propaganda organ, and this characterization would be legally actionable under the Corporate Expression Protection Ordinance of 2168. Instead, it operates under an 'Editorial Alignment Framework' that requires all broadcast content to pass through the Content Harmlessness Review Board (CHRB), a body with representatives drawn from the seven largest corporate shareholders. Stories touching on labor disputes, environmental contamination, citizenship grade appeals, or neural interface malfunction rates require CHRB pre-clearance before broadcast. Journalists who work within this framework are licensed professionals; journalists who do not are 'unlicensed content generators,' a status that carries civil liability for 'information disturbance' under the same ordinance.

The MNA's flagship program is 'The Daily Register,' broadcast at 0600, 1200, and 2200 across all tiers simultaneously, though tier-differentiated. In Tier-1 format, the Register runs forty-two minutes with eleven sourced segments and interactive query functionality. In Tier-4 format, it runs nineteen minutes, contains seven segments, and is non-interactive. The anchor team — currently Priya Olawale-Shen and Dmitri Vanek — are among the most recognizable faces in the megacity, their neural-linked expressions calibrated for trust-response optimization by the MNA's Audience Engagement Division. Their contracts prohibit them from speaking publicly on seventeen enumerated topics outside of broadcast contexts, including corporate acquisition disputes and citizenship reclassification policy.

For the majority of residents who consume news passively through ambient wall panels or neural ticker feeds, the MNA's output is simply 'the news' — undifferentiated from reality by any visible frame or disclaimer. The concept of editorial independence exists in the MNA's founding charter but is operationally subordinate to the Alignment Framework's requirements. Corrections are issued at a rate of 0.3 per broadcast cycle, a figure the MNA cites as evidence of accuracy. Critics who have studied the corrections database note that the corrected items are uniformly minor factual errors — dates, spellings, statistics — and that no correction has ever addressed a story's framing, sourcing gaps, or omission of corporate-adjacent information.
